description: A comprehensive study of the relationships between heat, work, temperature, and energy in Mechanical Engineering, encompassing the laws of thermodynamics and various power cycles.

sections.title: Basic Concepts and Zeroth Law
sections.description: Fundamental understanding of thermodynamic systems, properties, states, and the concept of thermal equilibrium.

key_concepts.explanation: An Open System allows the transfer of both mass and energy. A Closed System allows the transfer of only energy, not mass. An Isolated System permits neither mass nor energy transfer across its boundary.

Intensive properties are independent of the mass of the system (e.g., temperature, pressure, density). Extensive properties depend on the size or extent of the system (e.g., total volume, total internal energy).

States that if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body, they are also in thermal equilibrium with each other. This principle forms the foundational basis for temperature measurement.

sections.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
sections.description: The principle of conservation of energy and its specific application to closed systems and steady-flow control volumes.

equations: For a Closed System: dQ = dU + dW (where dQ is heat transfer, dU is change in internal energy, dW is work done)
Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE): h1 + (V1^2)/2 + gZ1 + q = h2 + (V2^2)/2 + gZ2 + w

results: For an ideal gas, the change in internal energy is strictly zero (dU = 0).
All heat added to the system is entirely converted into work done by the system (dQ = dW).
There is absolutely no heat transfer between the system and its surroundings.
Work done by the system is performed purely at the expense of its internal energy (dW = -dU).

sections.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy
sections.description: Understanding the directional nature of processes, the qualitative degradation of energy, and the concept of entropy.

key_concepts.explanation: It is impossible for any device that operates on a thermodynamic cycle to receive heat from a single thermal reservoir and produce a net amount of work. Some heat must be rejected to a lower-temperature sink.

It is impossible to construct a device that operates in a cycle and produces no other effect than the transfer of heat from a lower-temperature body to a higher-temperature body. Work input is required (basis of refrigerators and heat pumps).

A quantitative measure of the molecular disorder or randomness of a system. The principle of increase of entropy states that the entropy of an isolated system during a process always increases or, in the limiting case of a reversible process, remains constant.

sections.title: Pure Substances and Vapor Power Cycles
sections.description: Analysis of phase-change processes (water to steam) and the evaluation of the ideal Rankine cycle used in steam power plants.

steps.title: Pumping (Isentropic Compression)
steps.detail: Liquid water exiting the condenser is compressed to the high operating pressure of the boiler using a feed water pump.

steps.title: Heat Addition (Isobaric Heating)
steps.detail: High-pressure liquid water enters the boiler and is heated at constant pressure until it becomes superheated steam.

steps.title: Expansion (Isentropic Expansion)
steps.detail: The superheated steam expands through the steam turbine, dropping in pressure and temperature while generating mechanical shaft work.

steps.title: Heat Rejection (Isobaric Condensation)
steps.detail: The low-pressure exhaust steam from the turbine enters the condenser, where heat is rejected at constant pressure to convert it back into a saturated liquid.

sections.title: Gas Power Cycles
sections.description: Theoretical study of standard air cycles utilized in internal combustion engines and gas turbine systems.

results: The ideal standard cycle for spark-ignition (petrol) internal combustion engines.
Composed of two isochoric (constant volume) processes and two isentropic (reversible adiabatic) processes.
Thermal efficiency increases as the compression ratio (r) increases: n = 1 - (1 / r^(gamma - 1)).
The ideal standard cycle for compression-ignition (diesel) internal combustion engines.
Heat addition takes place at constant pressure, whereas heat rejection takes place at constant volume.
For the exact same compression ratio, the Otto cycle is always more efficient than the Diesel cycle.
The fundamental ideal cycle for gas turbine power plants and jet engines.
Composed of two isobaric (constant pressure) processes for heat addition/rejection and two isentropic processes for compression/expansion.
